title: Eight Weeks Out of Work
subtitle: An eight week plan from James Bell for anyone who has lost a job, laid off or fired. The first steps, the shame, the people at home, lament, a shape for the day, help received, the search, and work that isn't a god.
intro:
This is an eight week plan for you if you've lost a job, whether it ended in a short meeting and a box for your things, a phone call, or a business that closed. Each week holds one focus, one small daily practice, one thing to read, one tool to use, and one honest question. It moves slowly on purpose. It starts with the first practical steps and the shame that so often comes with them, turns to the people at home and to lament, the old prayer for loss, and ends with a shape for your days, help received without shame, the long search, and a way to hold work as a calling without making it a god. Losing a job is a real loss, and it's right to grieve it, but it isn't a verdict on your worth. Nothing here promises that the next job will come quickly or be better than the last.

It isn't a cure, and it isn't a substitute for a doctor, a licensed counselor, a pastor, or the people who love you. I'm a pastor, not a doctor, a lawyer, or a financial adviser, and nothing here is medical, legal, or financial advice; many of the rules for benefits and health coverage differ from state to state. If this loss has turned into hopelessness, or into thoughts of ending your life, call or text 988 now and tell someone near you. Walk the plan imperfectly. A missed week is not failure; you just pick it back up. Some days the whole practice will be getting dressed and making one call, and that counts.
careNote: If the heaviness hasn't lifted after a couple of weeks, or you're drinking more to get through the days, see a doctor; a licensed counselor can help with the grief and the shame. Find Help lists SAMHSA's helpline, and the Domestic Violence Hotline if someone at home has become threatening. In a crisis, call or text 988, or call 911 if you're in danger.

weeks.focus: The first week, one step at a time
weeks.why: The first days after a job ends can feel unreal, and yet the loss comes with deadlines that won't wait until you're ready: a claim to file, health coverage to sort out, bills that come due before any hiring manager calls back. You don't have to plan your whole future this week. Jesus told his followers, "Today has enough trouble of its own" (Matthew 6:34), so take one step at a time. If you were fired, or aren't sure you qualify for benefits, apply anyway and let the state decide; if you think you were let go illegally, talk with an employment lawyer or legal aid soon. The printable budget puts giving and saving before the bills, and what to give in a month like this is a question faithful Christians answer differently; the money care page sets out the views. None of this is legal or financial advice.
weeks.practice: Today, if you can, tell your spouse or one close friend everything, including what you're afraid of. Then take one step a day: apply for unemployment benefits with the state where you worked, even if you live in another, and answer every question exactly as it happened; ask your employer or plan when your health coverage ends and what your choices are; fill in a bare-bones budget; and call your lenders before a payment is missed, asking about hardship options and writing down what they agree to.

read.label: I lost my job, the care page these weeks walk more slowly, with this week's first steps set out one by one

tool.label: The printable monthly budget, with lines for what's coming in, giving, saving, the home, food, getting around, and each debt with its minimum

weeks.reflection: What am I most afraid of right now, and who is the one person I can tell all of it to this week?

weeks.focus: Shame, and what your worth rests on
weeks.why: Beneath the money sits a question that comes at night: am I still worth anything? Shame answers that you weren't good enough. If you were fired for something you did, own it and make right what you can, but owning a failure isn't accepting a verdict on your whole worth. Before Jesus preached or healed anyone, the Father said, "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!" (Matthew 3:17). The word came before the work, and so did the image of God you bear (Genesis 1:27). If shame has turned darker, into the thought that you're a burden or that your family would be better off without you, I'd rather ask plainly: are you having thoughts of ending your life? If you are, that thought comes from the pain, and it lies about how much you're needed. Call or text 988 now, and tell someone near you.
weeks.practice: Each morning, read Matthew 3:13-17 slowly and notice that the Father speaks before Jesus has done any of his public work. Each evening, write one line about where shame spoke that day and what it said, and beside it write what is true, including anything that is yours to own. Before the week ends, tell one person how the job ended, in plain words, instead of keeping it quiet.

read.label: Where Does Your Identity and Worth Come From? On the difference between a worth you achieve and a worth you receive

tool.label: Matthew 3 in the Study Bible, where the Father calls Jesus his beloved Son before his public work begins

weeks.reflection: Whose voice tells me I'm worth only what someone will pay me, and when did I start believing it?

weeks.focus: The marriage and the children under the strain
weeks.why: A job loss lands on the whole household. Your spouse may be as frightened as you are, and fear between two people often comes out as blame. Children read a parent's face for clues, and silence leaves them to imagine a reason worse than the truth, so keep their routines steady and the bills off their shoulders. The letter of James asks everyone to be "quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger" (James 1:19), and in a frightened house that takes daily practice. If anyone's anger at home has turned into threats or violence, or someone in the house is afraid, that is more than strain, and safety comes first: call 911 in danger, and the Domestic Violence Hotline, listed on the Find Help page, can help you make a plan; don't try couples counseling while someone is afraid.
weeks.practice: If you're married and safe with each other, set a calm hour for each of you to say what you're most afraid of, with no fixing and no blame, and keep money talk to one set time a week. Tell your children soon and simply that you lost your job, that it isn't because of anything they did, that they're loved, and that you'll take care of them. If you've been short with anyone at home, apologize out loud. If you live alone, tell one friend how you really are.

read.label: How to Lead Your Family When You Feel Like a Failure, on repenting out loud, coming back tomorrow, and pointing your children past yourself

tool.label: The Conflict Guide, which begins with what to do if you're afraid of the other person, then walks a money disagreement in five steps

weeks.reflection: What are the people at home afraid of right now, and have I given them room to say it without defending myself?

weeks.why: Naomi left Bethlehem in a famine with her husband and two sons, and in Moab all three died. A widow without sons had lost her living along with her family, and when she came home she asked the women of the town to call her Mara, which means bitter: "I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty" (Ruth 1:21). Scripture keeps her complaint without correcting it. Lament is that kind of prayer, an honest complaint from someone who is still talking to God. After Babylon burned Jerusalem, the poet of Lamentations wrote, "I have forgotten what prosperity is" (Lamentations 3:17), and only then, with nothing outside changed, called to mind mercies that are "new every morning" (Lamentations 3:23). Your loss is not Naomi's, but it's real, and it belongs in your prayers.
weeks.practice: Each day, read a few verses of Ruth 1 or Lamentations 3 aloud, slowly. Early in the week, write your own lament in the shape this week's reading gives: call on God by name, tell him what went with the job without softening it (the paycheck, the people, the place where you were needed), and ask for what you want. Add a line of trust only if it's true; if it isn't yet, leave the space blank. Pray it aloud after each day's reading.

read.label: How to Practice Lament, on the four movements of a lament and how to write your own

tool.label: Ruth 1 in the Study Bible, with notes on why Naomi asked to be called Mara, bitter

weeks.reflection: If I told God as plainly as Naomi did what this loss has taken from me, what would I say?

weeks.why: A job gave your days more than a paycheck. It gave you a reason to get up, a place where you were expected, people outside your family, and effort that counted for something, and losing it takes all of that at once. The days can lose their shape: late mornings, job sites refreshed in the middle of the night, evenings with nothing to end them. Looking for work is real work, and it goes better with set hours and a stopping point. When Israel lived on manna, they gathered it every morning, enough for that day (Exodus 16:21), and Jesus taught his followers to pray, "Give us this day our daily bread" (Matthew 6:11). A day can be received the same way, with its share of work and its limits, one morning at a time.
weeks.practice: Get up at your usual time and get dressed as if someone expected you. Begin by asking God for today's bread. Give the search a set block each weekday, for applications, calls, and one conversation with someone in your field, and then stop. Get outside and move each day, and see or call one person. End each day with five minutes in the Worry Journal, writing the one thing that's yours to do tomorrow and handing the rest to God. Keep one day this week free of the search.

read.label: How to Handle a Job Loss, on grieving honestly and on treating the search like a job, with hours and structure

tool.label: The Worry Journal, five minutes before bed to write down what's yours to do tomorrow and hand the rest to God

weeks.reflection: What did my job give my days besides a paycheck, and which of those things can I begin to give them again?

weeks.focus: Letting other people carry some of it
weeks.why: For many people the hardest part of losing a job is needing help, but Scripture doesn't shame people in need for receiving it. Israel's law told farmers to leave the edges of their fields and the gleanings of the harvest "for the poor and the foreign resident" (Leviticus 23:22). Ruth, a widow and a foreigner, gleaned so she and Naomi could eat, and Boaz told his workers, "do not insult her" (Ruth 2:15). Paul had learned contentment in hunger, yet he told the church that sent him a gift, "you have done well to share in my affliction" (Philippians 4:14). Unemployment benefits are insurance, and taking what your state says you're eligible for, honestly, is nothing to be ashamed of. If receiving feels shameful, we in the church have often taught that without meaning to, by honoring titles and success. I'm a pastor, and that charge includes me.
weeks.practice: Tell your pastor or small group what happened, and say plainly what would help: job leads, someone to read your résumé, a meal in a hard week, help with a bill. Ask whether the church has a benevolence fund. When help comes, receive it without apology, and write down each kindness and who gave it, so you can thank them and remember. Receiving isn't a debt, but being needed matters too, so each day look for one small way to help someone else that costs only time.

read.label: What Does Philippians 4:13 Really Mean? On a prisoner's thank-you note and the help he did not wave away

tool.label: Ruth 2 in the Study Bible, with notes on gleaning and on the kindness of Boaz beyond what the law required

weeks.reflection: What help have I been too ashamed to ask for, and what do I believe receiving it would say about me?

weeks.focus: The long search, without despair or desperation
weeks.why: In a long search every silence can sound like the old verdict. Ecclesiastes saw that results are not verdicts: "neither is the bread to the wise, nor the wealth to the intelligent, nor the favor to the skillful. For time and chance happen to all" (Ecclesiastes 9:11). Desperation grabs at any offer, including the scam that asks you to pay for the job or to deposit a check and send some back; send nothing. Despair numbs the wait with a drink, late sleep, and silence. If the heaviness has lasted two weeks or more, see a doctor. If drinking is how you get through, see one before you stop, since stopping suddenly after heavy drinking can be dangerous; the care page on drinking, I can't stop drinking or using, has SAMHSA's helpline at the top. If hope has turned into thoughts of ending your life, call or text 988 now.
weeks.practice: Each weekday, keep the search to its set hours: a few careful applications, one real conversation with someone in your field, and a short record of what you sent and whom you called. Before you answer any offer, check it for the two marks of a scam. When a rejection comes, tell God and one person instead of carrying it alone. Don't decide on a new career in your worst week. Each morning, read 2 Thessalonians 3:13 aloud and do only today's share of the search.

read.label: How to Wait on God, on refusing the two ways out of waiting, forcing it and numbing it, and doing the faithful next thing

tool.label: 2 Thessalonians 3 in the Study Bible, where this week's word to the weary follows the line about anyone unwilling to work, with notes on whom that line was for

weeks.reflection: When the search goes quiet, what do I start to believe about myself and about God, and is it true?

weeks.focus: Work as a calling, without making it a god
weeks.why: Work is older than the curse. Before anything had gone wrong, God placed the man in the garden "to cultivate and keep it" (Genesis 2:15), and Jesus spent most of his life in Nazareth, where his neighbors knew him as a tradesman: "Isn't this the carpenter" (Mark 6:3). Good work is one way of loving God and your neighbor, and it's right to want it back. But a job asked to tell you who you are has become a god, and that god fails everyone in the end, because every working life ends, by a layoff, an illness, or old age. In the New Testament, calling means first the call to belong to Christ (Romans 1:6), and no one can lay you off from it. A job can feed a family and give you a place to serve. It was never your name.
weeks.practice: Write on a card the two or three practices from these weeks that actually helped, such as the prayer for daily bread, the set hours and the stopping, or the weekly talk at home, and keep them whether or not the next job comes this month. Add one way you'll serve this week where you are, at church, at home, or for a neighbor. Show the card to one person and ask them to check on you in a month.

read.label: How to Discern Your Calling, on the call to belong to God that comes before any job, and on serving where you already stand

tool.label: The Rule of Life Builder, to choose a few practices across prayer, rest, the body, and service, and build a rhythm you can keep

weeks.reflection: If the next job is slow in coming, what will still be true about who I am, and where can I serve in the meantime?
